items.x_text:
GitBook says a "highly targeted attack using AI agents" reached its infrastructure credentials on 2 Nov. API tokens, Git Sync secrets and AI assistant questions may be exposed. Rotate GitBook tokens, replace integration secrets, re-auth MCP.

#AISecurity #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
GitBook says AI agents attacked it. 🤖

What we know (Decrypt, crypto.news, 3 Nov):
→ GitBook, a docs platform used by many crypto projects, says an attacker reached some infrastructure credentials on 2 Nov at 7 p.m. CET
→ It calls it "a sophisticated, highly targeted attack using AI agents". It hasn't said how the agents were used
→ Possibly exposed: API tokens, integration tokens and secrets, Git Sync secrets, and questions visitors sent to GitBook Assistant
→ GitBook says it found no evidence that any content was modified. It revoked personal API tokens and replaced its own credentials
→ PancakeSwap took its docs offline as a precaution and later moved them to its own infrastructure

What to do: rotate GitBook API tokens, replace any third-party tokens or secrets connected to GitBook (including published integrations), and re-authenticate the GitBook MCP server. Then check your repos for unexpected changes from Git Sync.

items.send_to: anyone on your team using mSecure

cover.hook: Your password manager emails you: change passwords, reset 2FA, remove passkeys.
cover.sub: mSecure's developer says it "recently learned of suspicious activity linked to the app". It hasn't said what happened.

slides.title: What the email says
slides.body: On 3 Nov, mSeven Software emailed current and former mSecure customers about suspicious activity linked to the app. It says it started an investigation, took steps to limit the problem and brought in outside security experts.

slides.title: What it doesn't say
slides.body: What happened, when, which systems, whether it has stopped, or whether vault data or the keys protecting it were reached. As of 18:00 UTC on 3 Nov there was no post on mSecure's X or Facebook (per The Hacker News).

slides.label: steps suggested: change passwords, reset 2FA, remove passkeys
slides.note: Offered as possibilities, with no order or detail (per The Hacker News)

slides.title: Why it matters
slides.body: mSecure 7 can store passkeys and 2FA codes in the vault (Essentials plan and above). If one app holds your passwords and your second factor, one incident touches both. mSecure says vault data is encrypted on the device before syncing.

slides.title: Do this today
items: Change email, bank and work passwords first
Move 2FA codes to a separate authenticator
Remove and re-create passkeys kept in mSecure
Expect phishing that mentions this incident

items.x_text:
mSecure password manager: developer mSeven emailed customers about "suspicious activity linked to the app" and suggested changing passwords, resetting 2FA and removing passkeys. It hasn't said what happened or if vault data was reached.

#DataBreach #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Your password manager emails you: change passwords, reset 2FA, remove passkeys. 🔑

What we know (The Hacker News, 3 Nov):
→ mSeven Software emailed current and former mSecure customers: it "recently learned of suspicious activity linked to the app"
→ It started an investigation, took steps to limit the problem and brought in outside security experts
→ It hasn't said what happened, when, whether it has stopped, or whether vault data or its keys were reached
→ It suggests changing passwords, resetting 2FA and removing passkeys, without saying which accounts come first
→ mSecure says vault data is encrypted on the device before syncing. mSecure 7 can also store passkeys and 2FA codes

What to do if you use it: change email, bank and work passwords first, move 2FA codes to a separate authenticator app, re-create passkeys, and treat any email about this incident with suspicion until mSecure publishes details.

items.x_text:
3AM ransomware and a suspected AI loop: Bitdefender says an affiliate hit a UK school estate, retrying failed commands every 40-101 s, likely via a language model. About 37 systems encrypted. Watch new domain trusts, protect backups.

#Ransomware #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Failed commands retried every 40 seconds. ⏱️

What Bitdefender found (via Hackread, 3 Nov):
→ A 3AM (ThreeAM) ransomware affiliate attacked one UK school estate in September: 47 systems across separate Active Directory domains
→ Failed commands were retried every 40 to 101 seconds. Bitdefender suspects command results were fed to a language model that suggested alternatives
→ It calls it a hybrid: a human at the keyboard plus a suspected agentic loop. It could not confirm the loop was automated
→ The attacker stole backup credentials, created backdoor admin accounts and new domain trusts, then tried to remove endpoint protection (blocked)
→ About 37 systems were encrypted and system-state backups deleted

What to do (Bitdefender): separate privileged accounts across domains, alert on new domain trusts, protect backup infrastructure, and make sure every machine has endpoint protection.

items.send_to: whoever owns your cloud AI budget
items.x_text:
LLMjacking explained: Google GTIG and Mandiant say stolen cloud keys are used to run and resell LLMs. Bills topped $100K in a day, up to $1M before access was cut. Fix: secret scanning, least privilege, spend caps, phishing-resistant MFA.

#AISecurity #CloudSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Stolen keys. Your AI bill. 💸

How LLMjacking works (Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant, 2 Nov):
→ Attackers get a key or token: leaked in a public repo, exposed in client-side code, phished, or from a misconfigured service account
→ They move in and stay: new access keys, new service accounts, more privileges
→ They use your models: token proxying, automated streaming, their own API keys
→ "LLM mixers" resell the access to underground subscribers. You pay the bill
→ The damage: over $100,000 in a single day in some incidents, up to $1 million before access was revoked
→ The tell: tiny test calls (like max_tokens=1) as attackers check stolen keys

Google's defences: secret scanning and rotation, least privilege (deny LLM access that isn't needed), API quotas and spending caps, phishing-resistant MFA.

#PatchNow #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
Old WinRAR bug. New spy campaign. 🗜️

What ESET reported (via The Hacker News, 3 Nov):
→ A Russia-aligned group ESET tracks as Gorbag exploits CVE-2025-8088, a patched WinRAR path-traversal flaw: a crafted archive writes files where the attacker chooses
→ Targets: Ukrainian law enforcement and justice bodies, local administrations near the front line, and defence
→ Lures: official-looking notices about fines and taxes
→ Malware: GIFTEDCROOK (steals browser data) and BeautyStealer
→ One script carried a comment telling AI and security tools it wasn't malicious. Two AI assistants still flagged it as a reverse shell

What to do: WinRAR has no built-in auto-updater, so find every copy and make sure it's on 7.13 or later. Treat archives from "official" senders with care.
